citations.quote: Abstract. An attitude determination and control system (ADCS) model is presented, which is used for CubeSat preliminary design stages in accordance with the European Space Agency (ESA) concurrent design approach. The model is implemented in Matlab/Simulink and integrated into the Concurrent Design Platform. The model's performance is exemplified by a mission preliminary design conducted in the Concurrent Engineering Lab at Skoltech.

Tracking the changes, keeping the documents consistent and up to date appeared to be quite expensive and error-prone. As a result, it is increasingly difficult to capture and trace the requirements from all the stages in system lifecycle during the development.

Concurrent design process is iterative in its nature. The team starts with rough models and rough parameter estimates and elaborates them from session to session in order to confirm or deny a particular hypothesis or to provide more accurate parameter estimate. Usually a goal for a particular session is announced in advance to increase the collaboration efficiency.

In CD software, the parametric model of the system is usually represented as a tree of parameters populated with values. Each subsystem is encoded by the corresponding subset of parameters (a branch of the tree). An example of the ADCS representation modeled in the CDP as part of this project is shown in Fig.1.

The ADCS design process is clearly delineated in classical textbooks on space mission analysis and design [14] and includes the following steps: - define control modes; - define or derive system-level requirements by control mode; - select type of spacecraft control by attitude control mode; - quantify disturbance environment; - select and size ADCS hardware (sensors and actuators); - define determination and control algorithms; - iterate and document.

Within the concurrent design approach, these steps are implemented by the ADCS team each time the corresponding inputs from other subsystems are changed (see Fig. 2). To track the changes in other subsystems' parameters influencing the ADCS design (the inputs), the CDP uses the mechanisms of subscriptions. A subscription is tied to the parameter of interest (which is a part of the overall system model) and automatically informs the ADCS team whenever this parameter has been changed.

For instance, Power-ADCS data exchange list contains the "bus voltage" parameter, whose value is communicated to the ADCS subsystem by the power subsystem. Vice versa, the ADCS subsystem notifies the power subsystem of the power consumption for each of the defined modes.

For example, an estimation of the average time each of the solar panels is lit by the Sun as the satellite is orbiting the Earth is hardly obtained merely through an expert's opinion and usually requires multiple simulations. Nevertheless, this particular estimate is important in the early design stages, as it may determine such critical structure design decision as whether the satellite must have deployable solar panels, which, in turn, substantially affects other subsystems.

In order to provide this computational capability, we developed a Matlab/Simulink ADCS model and integrated it with the parametric CDP ADCS model. The Matlab/Simulink model allows testing multiple hypotheses and examining multiple sets of parameters coming from the CDP model. The integration of the models allows automatic data exchange between them.
Power | Bus voltage; Solar array pointing required | ADCS consumption modes; Time solar panels are lit by the Sun

citations.quote: As our primary goal in using this model is to provide estimates for the ADCS performance, by default the most simple models are used to save the computation time, e.g. direct or tilted dipole model for the magnetic field, piecewise exponential approximation for the atmospheric density, constant Sun direction (determined by the start date), when only two or three orbital periods are simulated. If the need to make a refined analysis arises, these crude models can be substituted by more the complex ones, such as IGRF-12 for the geomagnetic field or NRLMSISE-00 for the atmospheric density.
The choice of the sensors from the CDP database results in automatic estimate of their consumption for all the regimes, in which the chosen sensors are active.

The model is implemented in Matlab/Simulink and is initialized directly from CDP. Thus, every time another subsystem undergoes any changes or a new hypothesis needs to be checked, the ADCS subsystem is informed of this, and the model is initialized with the up-to-date parameters' values. The model's output can also be imported into CDP and made known to other subsystems, which ensures the correct concurrent engineering procedures. The model's output is ADCS mass, ADCS attitude determination accuracy, characteristic detumbling time, characteristic pointing accuracy, characteristic power consumption in different regimes.

As a case study for preliminary ADCS design, we shall use one of the missions that was recently studied in the Skoltech Concurrent Enginering Lab. This is a technology demonstration mission involving a swarm of CubeSats. Each of the CubeSats is equipped with several gamma-ray detectors to register gamma-ray bursts (GRB) accompanying such events as mergers of neutron stars. The swarm includes four identical spacecraft, whose simultaneous observations of the sky from different positions should allow precise determination of a detected GRB direction.

The swarm is to be deployed from the International Space Station which defines the orbit and the environmental conditions used in the simulations. The spacecraft are not to be equipped with any kind of thrusters, so the guidance and navigation subsystem is missing from the list of teams, and its functions are partially given to the ADCS team. It was established during the concurrent design sessions that all the hardware needed (including 5 gamma ray sensors and all the subsystems) can be fit into a 3U CubeSat with non-deployable solar panels covering all the "large" sides and one "small" side (see Fig 4).

Estimates of the satellites initial spin rates vary in different sources and basically there is no reliable information on the initial conditions especially in the case of manual deployment (which is one of the considered options). There are evidences of the initial angular velocity being as high as 200 deg/s [17], in which case the gyroscope saturated and the mission had to be paused for nearly one year, while the angular velocity decreased for natural reasons (eddy-current torque). However, with the use of the special deployment mechanisms (such as P_POD) the initial spin rate does not exceed 20 deg/s [18]. Req1: The ADCS shall reduce the initial angular velocity below 1 deg/s.

The non-deployable solar panels are just barely enough to sustain the energy balance. This entailed the design of a safe-mode, in which only essential subsystems remain active for power saving, while the payload is shut down. The ADCS in this mode is allocated limited power resources and takes care of detumbling the spacecraft whenever its angular velocity grows greater than 1 deg/s. Going into this mode also requires coordination between the swarm members as it can be activated only in one of the four swarming satellites at a time and last for one orbital period. Thus, at any given time three of the four satellites in the swarm operate in the nominal mode with payload fully functioning, which should be enough to triangulate the detected GRB direction.
Req5: The ADCS uses minimum resources and goes into the detumbling mode if the value of the spacecraft's angular velocity becomes greater than 1 deg/s.

The whole detumbling process, as per this simulation, takes about two orbital periods. This ADCS performance characteristic is dependent on the power consumption regime, and can also become a point of compromise with the other subsystems.

In this simulation it takes approximately four orbital periods for the controller to achieve the desired attitude in the orbital reference frame. Having achieved it, the controller maintains the desired attitude as per Req3.

We showcased the use of CDP4 software to aid in the preliminary design procedures and in view of the necessity of providing additional means for fast modeling and simulation proposed our model to produce fast and reliable estimates of all the outputs expected of the ADCS team at the stage of the preliminary design.
It is, however, one of the plans for the future to incorporate into our model a possibility to run simulations with reaction wheels as well.

Therefore, it enables systems engineer to influence the decision process in case of conflicts between subsystems or interference with mission performance parameters.

Thus, preliminary design comes to models refinement in order to produce more accurate budget sheets as well as interface control specifications, where necessary. To facilitate the process it was chosen to use CDP4[12] software, which is generally a database of labeled parameters based on [13]. The standard defines data storage and communication ways for European space agencies. The software allows to define different roles and groups of users with different permissions that allow much flexibility in team structure. Generally, systems engineer has the control over all the parameters and has to approve all the changes to the model.

The system-level requirements for the nominal mode as formulated by the payload team are: Req2: The ADCS shall maintain zenith-pointing with the accuracy of $ \pm 1 5 $ deg. Req3: The ADCS shall provide attitude determination with the accuracy of 1 deg.
Req4: The ADCS shall prevent any of the large sides of the spacecraft to be exposed to the Sun for longer than one half of the orbital period.

The orbital motion model is reduced to the propagation of the Keplerian motion with the possible inclusion of the nodal precession due to the second harmonics of the geopotential. All other factors that influence the orbit evolution are neglected here, because the time, which it takes for this evolution to become significant, is much greater than the characteristic time sufficient to estimate the ADCS performance.
The value of the spacecraft's residual magnetic dipole is estimated as $ 0.01 \mathrm{~A} \cdot \mathrm{m}^{2} $ according to [19].

The Sensors block emulates the work of the sensors, such as magnetometers, gyroscopes, Sun sensors, star trackers. The characteristics of the sensors come from the COTs database. The sensors modeling takes into account the characteristic accuracy (including SNR specified in the documentation, sensitivity, and zero drift models), number and positions of the sensors (proceeding from the structure design subsystem), and the environmental factors (e.g.

the Sun sensor's signal depends on the spacecraft's attitude and position). The choice of the sensors from the CDP database results in automatic estimate of their consumption for all the regimes, in which the chosen sensors are active.
To this end the extended Kalman filter [16] is used with initial conditions obtained by the TRIAD algorithm.
